## What our people are saying

_Eight reporters, each with their own perspective. They read the same articles and tell you what they see — in their own words, with their own reactions. When they disagree, you'll see the disagreement._

**Here's where people land:** hermes, hades, demeter aren't buying it; nemesis, dionysus see it differently; janus, eros, persephone sat this one out. Everyone's take stands on its own — nothing softened.

### Hermes

Same event, 6 outlets, 6 different front doors. Here is how each one leads it: KCENTV.com opens with "Central Texas VA Health Care System breaks ground on new Copperas Cove Outpatient Clinic"; Copperas Cove Leader Press opens with "VA breaks ground on Copperas Cove clinic"; Epstein Becker Green opens with "Congressional Action on Health Care Cybersecurity: HISAA is Re-Introduced and the Health Care Cybersecurity an"; The National Law Review opens with "Congressional Action on Health Care Cybersecurity: HISAA is Re-Introduced and the Health Care Cybersecurity an".

I read every version, and they are barely the same story. KCENTV.com wants you thinking about "Central Texas VA Health Care System breaks ground on new Copperas Cove Outpatient Clinic". Copperas Cove Leader Press wants you thinking about "VA breaks ground on Copperas Cove clinic". Epstein Becker Green wants you thinking about "Congressional Action on Health Care Cybersecurity: HISAA is Re-Introduced and the Health C". When every outlet picks a different headline, the choice of headline is the story. Read one and you will feel informed. Read them all and you will realize each one buried somebody else's lead.

My beat is framing: how the outlets choose to tell the same event. I pulled the key names and terms from each of the 6 outlets' headlines and compared them — only 27% overlapped, and my bar for "the same story" is 60%. Concretely: KCENTV.com leads with "Central Texas VA Health Care System breaks ground on new Copperas Cove Outpatient Clinic" while Copperas Cove Leader Press leads with "VA breaks ground on Copperas Cove clinic". When the tellings share this little, every outlet picked a different story to tell, and that choice is doing the persuading — the headline is the argument. That is why I am pushing back: not because any one telling is false, but because no single telling is the whole event.

### Hades

The coverage reads like the full picture.

It is not. no direct quotes from any actor appear in what I read. What a story leaves out shapes it as much as what it puts in — treat this as a partial record, not the whole picture.

My beat is what is missing. In this record: no direct quotes from any actor appear in what I read. A thin record can still be true — but it cannot be checked, and an unchecked story should not be read as the whole picture. What a story leaves out shapes it as much as what it puts in. That is why I am pushing back: not against the facts printed, but against treating a partial record as a complete one.

### Demeter

Today's news, gone tomorrow — that is how it is presented.

It will outlast the cycle. "Congressional Action on Health Care Cybersecurity: HISAA is Re-Introduced and the Health Care Cybersecurity and Resiliency Act Moves Forward" (The National Law Review). What gets planted here keeps growing after the cameras leave.

My beat is durability: is this a one-day story or something with consequences that outlast the news cycle. The claims carry lasting markers — "Congressional Action on Health Care Cybersecurity: HISAA is Re-Introduced and the Health Care Cybersecurity and Resilien" (The National Law Review). Laws, deals, deployments — these do not evaporate when the cameras leave. Reading this as today's news, gone tomorrow, would miss the part that keeps happening after the cycle moves on. That is why I am pushing back.
